transcript.text: Incentives
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-02
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Predict behavioral responses and unintended consequences created by incentives.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Incentives change the expected benefits or costs of a choice, so they can alter behavior at the margin. A congestion fee raises the cost of the next downtown trip. Incentives can be monetary or nonmonetary, and different people may respond differently. A reward can also improve a measured result while harming the underlying goal.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A speed bonus makes workers finish faster, but quality falls.
A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road.
A toll is added to a crowded bridge, and some drivers switch routes.
A school rewards high test pass rates.
An incentive changes the payoff to a choice; it need not be monetary or guarantee a result.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to define incentives as cash payments or guaranteed behavior. An incentive changes the expected payoff to a choice; it may be monetary or nonmonetary, and people can respond differently.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RESPONDING TO INCENTIVES

A city adds a $4 congestion fee for a rush-hour trip. Assume other trip costs are already deducted from each driver's benefit. A driver with a remaining benefit of $3 avoids the trip because the fee exceeds that benefit. A commuter with a remaining benefit of $10 still travels. The fee changes choices at the margin without making every driver respond alike.
CHECK YOURSELF
A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-05
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish microeconomic and macroeconomic questions.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, workers, and individual markets. Macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment. One event can require both kinds of analysis. The distinction is the unit of analysis, not the size of an organization or dataset.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output.
A firm decides how much labor to hire at one restaurant.
Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.
A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase.
Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, and specific markets.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to label any large organization as macroeconomic. The classification depends on the unit of analysis: one decision-maker is micro; economy-wide aggregates are macro.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MICRO OR MACRO?

A restaurant deciding whether to hire one more server is a microeconomic question because it concerns one firm's choice. The national unemployment rate is a macroeconomic outcome because it aggregates labor-market conditions across the economy. The subject's size is not decisive; the unit of analysis is.
CHECK YOURSELF
A national retailer studies how its own customers respond to a price increase. Is that question microeconomic or macroeconomic, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Economists and Policy
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-10
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Analyze the economist's role in policy advice.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Economists use evidence and models to estimate policy effects, identify tradeoffs, and explain uncertainty. Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences. Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal. Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments. Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption.
Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.
A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period.
Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to give economists authority to choose society's values. Economists can estimate consequences and tradeoffs; the policy choice also requires normative judgments.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING POLICY ADVICE

An economist estimates that a proposed transit subsidy will increase ridership by 8%, but the estimate comes from a city with denser development. Professional advice reports the predicted benefit, explains the uncertain transfer to the local setting, and identifies fiscal costs. Whether those consequences justify the policy also depends on public values and priorities.
CHECK YOURSELF
An estimate from a dense city predicts an 8% ridership gain in a rural area. Which assumption about travel alternatives should the economist examine before applying that estimate?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
GDP Components
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The expenditure approach divides GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Consumption covers household purchases of final goods and services; investment includes business capital, residential construction, and inventory changes; government purchases pay for current goods and services. Net exports add exports and subtract imports so GDP counts only domestic production, while transfer payments themselves are excluded. A recipient's later purchase is counted separately if it pays for current domestic output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Classify final spending as consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports.
Count newly produced capital goods and inventory changes as investment.
Exclude transfer payments because they are not payments for current production.
Subtract imports within net exports so foreign production is not counted in domestic GDP.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to count transfer payments as government purchases. Transfers redistribute income and are never themselves part of GDP. A later purchase is classified by what is bought; imports are subtracted in NX.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING GDP EXPENDITURES

A business buys a newly produced domestic machine for $2 million; this is investment. Government pays contractors $80 million to repair roads; this is government purchases. An $80 million benefit payment is a transfer and is not counted when sent, though any later household purchase of final goods enters consumption. The expenditure identity classifies the counted spending as C + I + G + NX. These purchases contribute $2 million to I and $80 million to G, or $82 million directly to GDP; the transfer is not an additional government purchase.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Real versus Nominal GDP
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-03
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Nominal GDP values current production at current prices, while real GDP values it at base-year prices. Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods. GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare. Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Nominal GDP uses current-year prices and current-year quantities.
Real GDP uses base-year prices with current-year quantities.
A change in nominal GDP can reflect prices, quantities, or both; a change in real GDP reflects quantities.
Use the GDP deflator to compare nominal GDP with real GDP for the same year.
WATCH OUT
Do not use the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SEPARATING PRICE AND OUTPUT CHANGES

An economy produces 100 units in the base year at $5 each and 110 units this year at $6 each. Nominal GDP this year is 110 x $6 = $660. Real GDP at base-year prices is 110 x $5 = $550. The GDP deflator is ($660 / $550) x 100 = 120, separating the price increase from the output increase.
CHECK YOURSELF
Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Limits of GDP
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-04
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate GDP as a measure of well-being.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

GDP measures market production, not every dimension of well-being. GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off. GDP is useful, but it is not a complete measure of well-being. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently. GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals.
Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service.
A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours.
A free digital service replaces a paid service while users receive greater benefit.
A free technology replaces paid translation services, measured GDP falls, and users translate more text with less effort.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHAT GDP MISSES

A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding adds $2 billion to measured construction. Holding other domestic production constant, rebuilding adds $2 billion to GDP. It does not subtract the homes that were destroyed or the loss of security and leisure, so the GDP increase does not prove that well-being improved.
CHECK YOURSELF
A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding raises measured GDP. Name one loss the GDP increase does not subtract and explain why higher GDP does not prove higher well-being.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
CPI Bias
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-06
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Analyze substitution, quality, and new-goods bias.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A fixed-basket index can overstate growth in the cost of maintaining a living standard when buyers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods. Quality improvements and new goods also complicate price comparisons. These issues distinguish a change in posted prices from a change in the cost of obtaining comparable benefits.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist.
A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality.
A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RECOGNIZING CPI BIAS

A fixed basket contains beef even after beef prices rise sharply. Consumers substitute toward chicken, but the CPI continues pricing the original beef quantity. Because the fixed basket misses that cost-saving response, measured inflation can exceed the increase in the cost of maintaining consumers' actual purchasing pattern.
CHECK YOURSELF
A refrigerator sells for the same price but uses much less electricity and lasts longer. Which CPI issue matters?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
CPI versus GDP Deflator
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-07
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Compare the construction and uses of CPI and the GDP deflator.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The CPI tracks prices paid for a consumer basket, while the GDP deflator tracks prices of currently produced domestic final output. Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly. Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP. Identify the buyer and production location, then match the price change to the index whose scope includes it. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.
A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises.
Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged.
A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel.
Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE RIGHT PRICE INDEX

The price of imported coffee rises while prices of domestically produced goods are unchanged. Coffee is in the consumer basket, so the increase can raise CPI. Because the coffee was produced abroad, it is not part of domestic GDP and does not directly raise the GDP deflator.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Indexing and Real Values
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Convert nominal values across time and apply indexation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price index converts nominal amounts across time and can be used to index wages, benefits, rents, or tax thresholds. Converting an earlier nominal amount into later dollars requires multiplying by the later index divided by the earlier index. Indexation preserves purchasing power only when the chosen index and adjustment timing closely match the prices relevant to the recipient.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the nominal amount, the starting index, and the ending index.
Scale the nominal amount by the ratio of the ending index to the starting index.
Check whether the contract uses the same index and adjustment timing as the prices relevant to the recipient.
A fully indexed nominal payment preserves purchasing power only to the extent that the index matches actual costs.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INDEXING A NOMINAL PAYMENT

A salary was $40,000 when CPI was 100. CPI is now 160. 40,000 x 160/100 = 64,000.  Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why might a tax threshold be indexed to a price index?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Living Standards and Growth
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-10
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use real GDP per person and compounding to compare living standards.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Real GDP per person is a common measure of material living standards, and compounding makes sustained growth powerful over time. Dividing real output by population distinguishes growth in total production from growth in average material resources. Productivity growth can raise output per person without requiring proportionally more work, although this measure does not capture every dimension of well-being.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged.
Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.
Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards and growth.
Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.
Compare growth in real GDP with population growth to distinguish total output from output per person.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate more total labor input with higher productivity or complete welfare improvement. Productivity is output per unit of input, and GDP omits important dimensions of well-being.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPOUNDING LIVING-STANDARD GROWTH

If real GDP per person grows at 4% per year, the Rule of 70 estimates a doubling time of 70/4 = 17.5 years. This calculation describes material output growth, not complete well-being: longer work hours can raise GDP per person without raising output per hour or preserving leisure.
CHECK YOURSELF
Country A grows at 2% per year and Country B at 4%. Use the Rule of 70 to compare approximate doubling times. Why does a small growth-rate difference matter over decades?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Unemployment Measurement
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor-force status depends on work, job attachment, availability, and active job search. Employed people include those working for pay or profit, those temporarily absent from a job, and qualifying unpaid family workers. Unemployed people have no job, are available, and actively searched in the past four weeks; people awaiting recall from temporary layoff need not search. Discouraged workers who have stopped searching are outside the labor force.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Work for pay or profit during the reference week counts as employment, even if part-time.
At least 15 hours of unpaid work in a family business also counts as employment.
Labor force = employed + unemployed; unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force x 100.
Participation rate = labor force / civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older x 100.
WATCH OUT
Wanting a job alone does not make a person unemployed. Check job status, availability, and active search, including the temporary-layoff exception. Discouraged workers are outside the labor force.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING LABOR-FORCE STATUS

Among 100 people in the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older, 60 are employed, 5 are unemployed, and 35 are outside the labor force. Labor force = 60 + 5 = 65. Unemployment rate = 5/65 x 100 = 7.7%; participation rate = 65/100 x 100 = 65%.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which two groups are added to calculate the labor force?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Types of Unemployment
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Frictional unemployment comes from ordinary job search, structural unemployment from lasting mismatches, and cyclical unemployment from recessions. Layoffs caused by recession are cyclical unemployment. Short-term search between jobs is frictional unemployment. Job loss from weak demand during a recession is cyclical unemployment. A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A worker loses a job because a recession causes customers to spend less.
A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills.
Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.
Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.
A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse the cause of unemployment with official labor-force status. For a jobless worker who is available and actively searching, normal search after leaving a job is frictional unemployment; recession-related job loss is cyclical unemployment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING UNEMPLOYMENT TYPES

A worker leaves a job and spends six weeks searching for a better match; that is frictional unemployment. A factory worker whose skills no longer match available technology faces structural unemployment. A restaurant worker laid off because a recession reduces spending experiences cyclical unemployment.
CHECK YOURSELF
A worker's occupation disappears after a lasting technology change, and their skills do not match new vacancies. Which type of unemployment is this, and how does it differ from ordinary job search?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Money Functions and Measures
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify money's functions, forms, and M1/M2 measurement.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. As a medium of exchange it facilitates purchases; as a unit of account it provides a common way to quote prices and debts; as a store of value it carries purchasing power into the future. Money-supply measures group liquid assets by how readily they can perform these functions.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A medium of exchange is used to buy and sell goods and services.
A unit of account provides the common measure in which prices and debts are stated.
A store of value transfers purchasing power from the present into the future.
For a money-supply measure, classify an asset by its liquidity and the measure's stated definition.
WATCH OUT

A transfer from a checking deposit to a retail money-market fund lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged. Checking and savings deposits are included in both under the stated post-2020 definition; retail money-market funds are only in M2.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLASSIFYING MONEY-SUPPLY MEASURES

Currency is $800, checking deposits are $1,200, and savings deposits are $1,500. Under the U.S. definition used since May 2020, savings deposits are included in M1, so M1 = $3,500. With no other M2 components, M2 is also $3,500. Under the older textbook definition excluding savings from M1, M1 would be $2,000.
CHECK YOURSELF
Are retail money-market mutual funds included in M1, M2, or both?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-19
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain central-bank structure, roles, independence, and the FOMC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy, supplies reserve balances, supports payments, and serves as lender of last resort. Its structure includes the Board of Governors and 12 regional Reserve Banks; the FOMC directs monetary policy. Operational independence allows policy decisions without day-to-day political approval within a mandate set by Congress. The Treasury manages federal finances rather than monetary policy.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
The FOMC sets the monetary-policy stance and directs open-market operations.
A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions.
A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account.
Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution. Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CENTRAL BANK OR TREASURY?

The Federal Reserve buys Treasury securities from a bank, adding reserve balances. In the limited-reserves textbook model, this tends to lower short-term rates; in an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main rate-control tool. The purchase is monetary policy, not a change in federal taxes or spending.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which group directs open-market operations?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monetary-Policy Tools
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-21
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply open-market operations, administered rates, and reserve tools.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The Federal Reserve influences bank reserves, the money supply, and short-term interest rates through several policy tools. Open-market purchases add reserves to the banking system, while open-market sales remove them. Administered rates change the incentives banks face when borrowing or holding reserves. Changes in reserves can affect bank lending and deposit creation, although the actual expansion of money may be smaller than the simple textbook multiplier predicts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
An open-market purchase adds reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to lower short-term rates.
An open-market sale removes reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to raise short-term rates.
Lower administered rates ease monetary conditions; higher administered rates restrain them.
In an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main tool for controlling short-term rates.
WATCH OUT
More reserves do not guarantee a fixed expansion of broad money. Banks, borrowers, and depositors affect the response; the simple multiplier is a separate restrictive model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MATCHING THE TOOL TO ITS EFFECT

A $50 million security purchase adds $50 million of reserves. In a limited-reserves textbook market, that tends to lower short-term interest rates. In an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main rate-control tool. Distinguish each tool's immediate effect from the eventual lending and spending response.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Limits of Monetary Control
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate currency drain, excess reserves, leverage risk, and multiplier slippage.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The central bank influences broad money, but banks and the public also determine lending, deposits, and currency holdings. Excess reserve holding and currency drain weaken the simple deposit-expansion process. Banks with little capital may be especially cautious about losses and lending. These choices prevent a mechanical link from new reserves to a fixed amount of broad money.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.
When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.
The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.
The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves.
Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money. The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MONEY EXPANSION FALLS SHORT

The Fed adds $40 million of reserves, but banks hold half as excess reserves and the public keeps some funds as cash. Because only part of the injection supports new loans and redeposits, broad money rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts. The Fed controls reserves more directly than it controls deposits held by the public. A bank with a thin capital cushion may also limit new lending to reduce its exposure to losses.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monetary Neutrality
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-24
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real variables and analyze long-run neutrality.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Monetary neutrality means that a lasting change in the money supply changes nominal variables but not real output or employment in the long run. Nominal variables changed, but real output did not. Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run. Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Separate nominal variables, measured in money, from real variables, measured in goods, services, or purchasing power.
A lasting money-supply change can alter the price level and other nominal values in the long run.
Under monetary neutrality, long-run real output and employment remain determined by real resources and technology.
Do not apply long-run neutrality to the short run, when sticky prices can make money affect real activity.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume money changes real variables permanently in the long run. Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NOMINAL VERSUS REAL EFFECTS

Under the stated long-run neutrality assumptions, doubling money doubles prices and nominal wages. The real wage is unchanged: $20 / $5 = 4 units per hour before and $40 / $10 = 4 afterward. Real output remains 100 units. Nominal amounts change while real purchasing power and productive capacity do not.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Costs of Inflation
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-26
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze redistribution, shoeleather costs, menu costs, and price distortions.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between borrowers and lenders on fixed nominal contracts. Even expected inflation can create costs: changing posted prices uses resources (menu costs), economizing on cash takes time and effort (shoeleather costs), and uneven price changes can obscure relative-price signals.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Unexpected inflation lowers the real repayment on a fixed nominal debt.
Menu costs are resources spent changing posted prices.
Shoeleather costs arise from efforts to hold less money during inflation.
Relative-price confusion can make economic decisions harder.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse shoeleather costs with menu costs. Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: UNEXPECTED INFLATION REDISTRIBUTION

A lender makes a 9% loan expecting 3% inflation, so the expected real return is approximately 6%. Actual inflation turns out to be 10%, making the realized real return approximately 9% - 10% = -1%. Unexpected inflation transfers purchasing power from the lender to the borrower.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-42
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate private, public, and national saving in closed and open economies.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

With net taxes T, private saving is Y - T - C and public saving is T - G. National saving is their sum: S = Y - C - G. In a closed economy, S = I. In an open economy, S = I + NCO; because NX = NCO in the course model, S = I + NX. These are aggregate identities, not claims that each saver directly funds one investor.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Budget surplus means T - G is positive; a deficit makes public saving negative.
Adding private and public saving cancels T and gives Y - C - G.
Use S = I only for the closed-economy model.
In an open economy, saving can finance domestic investment or net capital outflow.
WATCH OUT
Do not reverse the public-saving sign. T - G is public saving; G - T is the budget deficit. Also state the closed-economy assumption before writing S = I.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FROM COMPONENTS TO OPEN-ECONOMY SAVING

Let Y = $1,200, T = $150, C = $760, and G = $260. Private saving is $290; public saving is -$110; national saving is $180. If domestic investment is $140, then NCO = S - I = $40. The accounting identity also gives NX = $40.
CHECK YOURSELF
Private saving is $220 and public saving is -$50. What is national saving?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Deficits, Debt, and Government Borrowing
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-47
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish annual budget flows from accumulated public debt.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget deficit occurs when government outlays exceed revenues during a period; it is financed by borrowing and tends to add to public debt. A surplus can reduce debt if used for repayment. Debt is the accumulated stock of outstanding borrowing, not the current year's deficit. Borrowing can finance valuable investment or current spending, so its effects depend on use, scale, interest costs, and economic conditions.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Deficit: one period's negative budget balance; debt: outstanding stock at a date.
New borrowing generally rises with a deficit and adds to debt.
Interest payments can absorb future budget resources.
Lower public saving links deficits to loanable funds and possible crowding out.
WATCH OUT

Debt is a stock, not this year's deficit or the sum of all past spending. When a deficit is measured using total outlays, interest is already included: do not add it again when updating debt. Other accounting adjustments may also matter.

HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A movement along one short-run Phillips curve reflects a change in aggregate demand with expected inflation fixed.
Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
An adverse supply shock can shift the curve upward by raising inflation at each unemployment rate.
Compare inflation at the same unemployment rate to identify a shift rather than a movement along the curve.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse a curve shift with movement along one curve. At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING THE PHILLIPS CURVE

Horizontal axis: unemployment rate; vertical axis: inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower, leftward downward-sloping curve; SRPC2 is the higher, rightward downward-sloping curve. Point a on SRPC1 is at unemployment U1 and inflation I2. From left to right the unemployment labels are U1, U2, U3; I2 is above I1. Dashed guides identify all four points. No numerical rates are printed.

The economy begins at point b on SRPC2 with unemployment U2 and inflation I2. When expected inflation falls, the short-run Phillips curve shifts downward to SRPC1. At the natural unemployment rate U2, the economy reaches point c with lower inflation I1. Expectations, not a permanent unemployment change, drive the shift.

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.

Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.

Identify the fixed basket, its base-year cost, and its current-year cost.
Compute the price index by comparing the current basket cost with the base-year basket cost.

The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.

THE CORE IDEA

Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden; identify that side from the market conditions.
A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in quantity but a large increase in buyer price.
In one market, demand is much more elastic than supply.

Fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through changes in government purchases, taxes, and their effects on consumption. Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left. A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

Higher government purchases directly raise aggregate demand; lower purchases reduce it.
Tax changes affect aggregate demand indirectly by changing disposable income and consumption.
Expansionary fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand right; contractionary policy shifts it left.
Distinguish a shift of aggregate demand from a movement along the curve caused by the price level.

A common mistake is to classify fiscal policy from the economy's condition rather than the government's action. Higher purchases or lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases or higher taxes are contractionary.

The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural unemployment rate because expected inflation eventually adjusts. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions.

Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.

An import quota directly limits the quantity of a good that may enter the country. A binding quota reduces imports below their free-trade level, raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption. The price gap between the domestic quota price and the world price creates quota rent. Who receives that rent affects the country's national-surplus result, while the production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Begin with the free-trade outcome at the world price.
A binding import quota limits imports below their free-trade quantity.
The restriction raises domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption.
The gap between the quota price and world price creates quota rent on each permitted import.
Look for deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.

Do not assume quota rent automatically becomes government revenue. It accrues to whoever holds the import rights; auctioning those rights can transfer the rent to government. The recipient matters for national welfare, while production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.

At $3, supply is 75 thousand and demand is 275 thousand; at $6, supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

Before trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at a price of $7. With free trade, buyers can purchase at the $3 world price, which creates imports. The quota limits imports, so the domestic price rises to $6. The difference between the $6 quota price and the $3 world price is $3 per imported unit; that $3 gap is quota rent.

When velocity is stable and real output is determined by productive capacity, persistent money growth above real-output growth produces long-run inflation rather than permanently higher real output.

The problem uses MV = PY or relates money growth to inflation.
Velocity measures how often money supports transactions during a period.
With velocity and real output fixed, more money raises the price level.
The question distinguishes a nominal price change from a lasting real-output change.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume money growth permanently raises real output. The quantity theory connects persistent money growth to inflation, especially in the long run.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MONEY GROWTH AND INFLATION

Quantity-theory graph. The vertical axis is value of money, one divided by P; the horizontal axis is money supply M. Money demand MD slopes downward and curves toward the horizontal axis. Vertical MS1 is at 2,500 and meets MD at point a, at a money value of 2. Vertical MS2 is at 5,000 and meets MD at point b, at a money value of 1. Dashed horizontal guides mark 2 and 1. MS2 is to the right of MS1 and b is below and to the right of a. The vertical axis shows the reciprocal of the price level, not velocity V.

In this clean quantity-theory case, velocity V and real output Y are fixed. Money supply doubles from 2,500 (MS1) to 5,000 (MS2). The value of money falls from 2 at a to 1 at b. Since P is its reciprocal, P rises from 1/2 = 0.50 to 1/1 = 1.00: a 100% increase. The graph shows value of money (1/P), not velocity V in MV = PY.
CHECK YOURSELF
With velocity and real output fixed, money grows by 10%. What happens to the price level in this quantity-theory example, and why does real output not rise?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Phillips Curve
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-37
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment when expected inflation is fixed. With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC. The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run. The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment.
Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.
The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
A move up and left along the displayed SRPC means lower unemployment and higher inflation.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model. The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG THE SRPC

Horizontal axis: unemployment rate in percent; vertical axis: inflation rate in percent. Downward-sloping SRPC0 intersects vertical LRPC at A, unemployment 5 percent and inflation 2.5 percent. Dashed guides connect A to the axes. SRPC0 extends above A to the left and below A to the right. LRPC remains at 5 percent unemployment.

Point A has 5% unemployment and 2.5% inflation. With expected inflation fixed, stronger aggregate demand moves the economy up and left along this same SRPC: unemployment falls while inflation rises. Weaker demand moves it down and right. A change in expectations would instead shift the curve.
CHECK YOURSELF
On a Phillips graph, moving upward and left along one SRPC means what?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Open-Economy Policy and Macroeconomic Transmission
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-57
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Trace fiscal and financial shocks through saving, NCO, FX, NX, and AD.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

Use one chain at a time. In this model, a larger budget deficit reduces national saving and raises the real interest rate. Domestic assets become more attractive, so net capital outflow (NCO) falls. Fewer dollars are supplied for foreign assets, the dollar appreciates, and net exports fall. The FX graph holds price levels fixed and uses vertical dollar supply determined by NCO, unlike the basic gross-flow graph on MACRO-56.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Less national saving can raise the real interest rate.
A higher domestic real rate lowers NCO.
Lower NCO shifts vertical dollar supply left.
Dollar appreciation reduces net exports, holding price levels fixed.
WATCH OUT
Do not claim a fixed quantitative offset or that every fiscal expansion changes output by the same amount. The model identifies directions; magnitudes depend on responses across markets.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FROM A DEFICIT TO NET EXPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of U.S. dollars exchanged; vertical axis: exchange rate in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Downward-sloping D0 = NX0 meets solid vertical S0 = NCO0 at A, quantity 100 and rate 1.0. Dashed vertical S1 = NCO1 lies to the left at quantity 50 and meets the same demand curve at B, rate 1.5. Dashed horizontal guides mark both rates. The supply lines are vertical in this panel.

Suppose a deficit raises the real rate and lowers NCO. In the graph, dollar supply falls from NCO0 = 100 to NCO1 = 50. Equilibrium moves from A to B, and the exchange rate rises from 1.0 to 1.5 foreign units per dollar. Dollar appreciation reduces NX; higher rates also crowd out some investment.
CHECK YOURSELF
Capital flight raises NCO. Trace the likely directions of dollar supply, the dollar's value, and NX.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

transcript.text: Tax Wedges and Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
WATCH OUT
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax times the quantity actually traded after the tax. Use the $6 wedge and 80 units here; do not multiply by the original untaxed quantity.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TAX REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price in dollars. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up, intersecting demand at quantity 100 and price 15. A parallel Supply + tax curve above supply intersects demand at quantity 80 and price 18. At quantity 80, original supply is at price 12. Dashed guides also mark prices 10 and 20 and quantities 65, 120 and 150.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ELASTICITY AND REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. A straight downward-sloping Demand line runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Its marked points are C at quantity 30, price 12; B at quantity 60, price 8; and A at quantity 90, price 4. Dashed guides show each point on both axes.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
CHECK YOURSELF

Cruise-cabin price falls from $3,200 to $2,880 while quantity rises from 1,500 to 1,900. Calculate midpoint elasticity and both revenue totals. Is demand elastic over this range, and does revenue rise or fall?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
WATCH OUT
Producer surplus is the price received minus willingness to accept, summed over units sold. Do not confuse this per-unit price-cost gap with total revenue.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING PRODUCER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
WATCH OUT
Total surplus adds consumer and producer surplus. A payment between buyers and sellers changes its distribution; a trade whose cost exceeds buyer value reduces total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TOTAL SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficient Quantity & Allocation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Efficient Quantity & Allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
WATCH OUT
More output is not always more efficient. Stop when the next unit costs more to produce than its buyer is willing to pay.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE EFFICIENT QUANTITY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 18 at quantity 0 and reaches price 2 at quantity 16. Upward-sloping S starts at price 2 and reaches price 18 at quantity 16. They intersect at E, quantity 8 and price 10, with dashed guides to the axes. Demand lies above supply to the left of E and below supply to its right.

Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.
CHECK YOURSELF

Five buyers value one pass each at $27, $23, $18, $13, and $8. Five sellers have costs of $4, $10, $15, $21, and $25. How many trades create nonnegative gains, and why should the next trade not occur?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT

When the world price exceeds the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. The difference is exports, not imports. Do not infer tariff revenue or deadweight loss from this free-trade example.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING EXPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the avocado export-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and exports at Pw=$10?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-32
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING SHORT-RUN FIRM SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: firm quantity; vertical axis: cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR is at 10, below the entire AVC curve. MC crosses minimum AVC at A, quantity 22 and cost 20. Other marked points on rising MC are B near quantity 36 and cost 30, C near quantity 44 and cost 41 at minimum ATC, and D near quantity 50 and cost 50. Unprinted coordinates are approximate. ATC is above AVC.

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 36 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-40
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Compared with competition, monopoly usually restricts output, raises price, transfers surplus, and creates deadweight loss. Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not. The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare monopoly output and price with the competitive benchmark where price equals marginal cost.
Monopoly normally produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
Separate the transfer of surplus to the monopolist from surplus lost through reduced output.
Deadweight loss is the value of trades between monopoly output and the efficient quantity that no longer occur.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to reverse monopoly competitive comparison. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING MONOPOLY DEADWEIGHT LOSS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down, and MR slopes down more steeply from the same vertical intercept. MC is horizontal at 20. MR meets MC near quantity 45; at that quantity, guides mark demand price about 47 and ATC about 24. Demand meets MC at quantity 90 and price 20; ATC there is slightly above 20. ATC declines throughout the displayed relevant range. The marked demand price at 45 is approximately 47.

The unregulated monopoly chooses about 45 units where MR = MC and charges the demand price of about $47. The efficient outcome occurs where demand meets MC: 90 units at $20. Monopoly therefore restricts output and raises price, leaving mutually beneficial units between 45 and 90 unproduced.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-44
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
WATCH OUT
Separate profit from shutdown. A fixed-cost increase can create an economic loss without changing marginal cost or the benefit of operating; compare revenue with variable cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN FIRM DECISION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The displayed baseline has Q = 36 and P = ATC = $27, so economic profit is zero. Consider a higher fixed lease cost of $108, with demand and variable costs unchanged. Output and price stay at that baseline, but ATC rises by $3 and the loss is $108. The firm still operates if revenue covers variable cost; loss alone does not imply shutdown.
CHECK YOURSELF
A firm earns a loss because P is below ATC. What additional cost comparison is needed to decide whether it should shut down in the short run?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-45
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

Short-run profit attracts competing varieties, reducing demand for each incumbent. Adjustment continues until demand is tangent to ATC at the chosen output. The graph shows that endpoint at 36 units and $27, where revenue and cost both equal $972. Tangency eliminates economic profit; it does not put output at minimum ATC.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does excess capacity measure?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
WATCH OUT
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MARKET CONCENTRATION

Horizontal axis: Firm or fringe, with categories A, B, C, D and Other; vertical axis: Market share in percent. The five bars have printed values A 38 percent, B 32 percent, C 12 percent, D 9 percent, and Other 9 percent. Other is a separate aggregate category, not labeled as a single firm.

The named firms contribute 38^2 + 32^2 + 12^2 + 9^2 = 2,693 HHI points. The remaining 9% is labeled Other, an unspecified fringe. If it were one firm, it would add 9^2 = 81 points. Thus 2,774 is an upper bound, not an exact HHI. An exact calculation requires the individual fringe shares.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can an aggregate Other category not generally be squared as if it were one firm when calculating exact HHI?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-51
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

In a sequential game, one player acts before another. Work backward from the last decision: identify the action that the later player will actually prefer, then use that response to evaluate the first move. A threat is credible only if carrying it out would be worthwhile when the decision arrives. Repeated interaction can make future consequences matter, but no present-value calculation is needed here.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
WATCH OUT
A threatened response is not automatically credible. Compare the later player's payoffs at the decision point before using the threat to predict the first move.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A CREDIBLE THREAT

Sequential game tree; payoffs are ordered Entrant, Incumbent. The Entrant moves first. Stay out ends with payoffs (0, 12). Enter leads to the Incumbent decision node. From that node, Accommodate ends with (6, 7), and Fight ends with (negative 3, 3). Branch labels identify the actions; each payoff belongs to its branch endpoint.

The game tree is solved backward. If entry occurs, the incumbent receives 7 by accommodating and 3 by fighting, so accommodation is the credible response on that branch. Anticipating it, the entrant compares 6 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The backward-induction outcome is Enter, then Accommodate.
CHECK YOURSELF
After entry, why will the incumbent accommodate rather than fight, and how does that affect the entrant's first decision?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Factor Markets & Labor Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-57
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal productivity to analyze labor demand, wages, and employment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor demand is derived from the value workers add to output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker. For a price-taking seller, VMP = output price x MPL. A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where VMP equals the wage.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A wage change causes movement along labor demand; productivity or output-price changes shift labor demand.
Higher product demand, output price, or worker productivity shifts labor demand right.
Worker preferences, population, migration, training, and alternative jobs can shift labor supply.
Competitive wage and employment occur where market labor demand intersects market labor supply.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse MPL with VMP. MPL is extra physical output; VMP converts that output into dollars by multiplying by the output price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPETITIVE LABOR-MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Horizontal axis: hundreds of warehouse workers; vertical axis: hourly wage in dollars. Labor Demand slopes down from wage 30 at quantity 0 to zero at 120 hundreds. Labor Supply slopes up from wage 10. They intersect at wage 20 and quantity 40 hundreds of workers, with dashed guides to both axes. Supply lies above demand to the right of that intersection.

Suppose output sells for $5 and the marginal worker adds 4 units per hour. VMP is $5 x 4 = $20 per hour, matching a $20 wage. The graph shows market equilibrium at that wage and 40 hundreds of workers, or 4,000 workers. A higher output price raises VMP at each employment level and shifts labor demand right.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the output price rises while worker productivity is unchanged, what happens to labor demand?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Consumer Choice
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-58
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows affordable bundles at given income and prices. Its intercepts show the most of either good a consumer can buy. An indifference curve connects bundles the consumer ranks equally. The best affordable bundle reaches the highest available preference level; in this example, its curve just touches the budget line.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
Compare the highest preference curve that can be reached without exceeding the budget.
WATCH OUT
Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BEST AFFORDABLE BUNDLE

Horizontal axis: Good X; vertical axis: Good Y. A straight budget line runs from 40 units of Y at X = 0 to 20 units of X at Y = 0. Marked bundle A is X = 10 and Y = 20. At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.
CHECK YOURSELF
If only the price of Y falls, does the budget line shift in parallel or pivot?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
